messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: formula for RMSEA with missing data
parts:
On 10/06/2013 07:41 AM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> Hello Yves,
>
> I was wondering how RMSEA was calculated when there are missing data and
> FIML is the estimator. Do you use the number of rows in the data as N,
> or do you use a scaling factor, like is used to adjust the test
> statistic with MLR?

If estimator="MLR", you get two RMSEAs: the usual one (based on standard
X2) and one based on the scaled X2. The latter one uses an adjusted
value for the degrees of freedom:

# usual
RMSEA <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/df - 1/(N-GG), 0) ) ) * sqrt(G)

# scaled
RMSEA.scaled <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/d - 1/(N-GG), 0) ) ) * sqrt(G)
# where d <- sum(object@Fit@test[[2]]$trace.UGamma)

But both currently (0.5-14) use 'N' (as in the total number of rows in
the data). Perhaps this needs revision. Do you know of a paper
discussing this?

Yves.

I don't think so, at least nothing yet.  I'm reviewing some literature with my advisor to prepare for a simulation study comparing methods of model-evaluation with missing data, and she wondered whether any software packages used an "adjusted" or "effective" sample-size instead of nrow(data) for RMSEA.

We're also curious whether you have any plans to include Bollen-Stine bootstrap capabilities when there are missing data, using either of the promising techniques proposed by Savalei & Yuan (2009) -- attached.  These are among the methods we'd like to consider, but their software support is merely running EQS, importing the results into R, and running the algorithms manually.  (Of course, this is easily adaptable by extracting the same information from the lavaan object, so we can certainly still utilize their R syntax for our simulation.)  Mplus does bootstrapping when there are missing data, but the manual merely says that "Residual bootstrap is the Bollen-Stine bootstrap" -- which I'm not sure is the case, but regardless, I can't find any other details on their site discussing how they implement it.

Anyway, no need for any changes, I was just curious.  I probably should have just searched your source code for the answer about RMSEA to save you time, but I had just posted another question about the baseline model, and I had this on my mind.

Thanks!

Terry

Yves,

After looking more closely at the accompanying R syntax for Savalei & Yuan (2009), it seems like it may be easy to adapt it into a function for semTools.  I'm working on this simulation presently, so I'm going to write a function that accepts raw data and model-implied moments (potentially fit outside of R), does one of the 3 transformations (a user-specified argument), and returns bootstrapped samples, optionally with an option to export data to file(s) for analysis in another package.  Then I'll write a wrapper which allows the user simply to fit the target model to the data, and then pass the fitted lavaan object to the wrapped function (or OpenMx object).  Since their new method is not widely available (still only in EQS?), it would be a flexible tool for applied researchers using any software, including lavaan.  And that might save you some time for other developments :-)  Of course, if you still want to include this functionality in lavaan, I wouldn't complain, but I could also make a wrapper for the wrapper, which accepts model syntax and data, along with other lavaan arguments (similar to the runMI functions), and has extra arguments for which transformation, max iterations, etc.

If I don't run into any trouble, I should make a push to github within the next week.  Thanks for all your work!

Terry

Yes. They are estimated using the EM algorithm.

But you can 'extract' these from a fitted lavaan object by using
inspect(fit, "sampstat")

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: formula for RMSEA with missing data
parts:
For anyone interested in a model-based bootstrap (a la Bollen-Stine) with missing data, I've developed a function for semTools that employs the methods described in Savalei & Yuan (2009).  The regular lavaan user can simply fit the model to data with MAR observations using FIML, then feed that lavaan object to the bootstrapMissing() function and specify the number of bootstrap samples and which transformation to use (see details in Savalei & Yuan, 2009).  The function returns an S3 class "bootMiss" list object, which contains a time-stamp for the transformation and for the fitting of the model to the bootstrap samples, the transformed data itself, the bootstrap distribution of chi-squared values, and the bootstrap p value.  Users of other software can still utilize this function by supplying raw data and model-implied covariance/means instead of a lavaan object, and they can request only the transformed data (to bootstrap themselves) or a list of bootstrap samples, with the option to write either to a file for use in another program.

This will be available in semTools eventually, but I'd appreciate any feedback you have before the next update is released.  There are also print, summary, and plot methods, which you can inspect in the source code and the working examples.  I can't get Transformation 3 working -- fitting the model to the resulting data does not return a chi-squared = 0.  I'm working from the examples on Savalei's web page, and I'm not sure the transformation-3 code there matches the equations in the article.  I will need to contact the authors about what I'm doing wrong, but transformations 1 and 2 work fine.

Thanks,

Terry

Hi Terry and Yves,

I was wondering if there have been further developments related to the original posting question: a formula for the RMSEA with missing data. I have a dataset with a lot of missing data (only a few variables have full data while most variables have 50% missingness) and feel that the regular RMSEA formula after FIML estimation is overestimating the "true" model fit due to using the number of cases with any data. I have considered replacing N in the formula with the listwise deletion N (which seems too strict) or the average of the pairwise deletion Ns (which seems more reasonable). Any thoughts?

-David
